newsitem.title: UK: POLL - UK Labour keeps huge lead in Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: POLL - UK Labour keeps huge lead in Reuters poll.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party has a 22-point lead over the ruling Conservatives and is lining up to win the biggest seat majority any party has enjoyed in parliament since 1924, an NOP poll for Reuters forecast on Wednesday.

The lead for Labour is one percentage point ahead of a previous NOP poll for Reuters three weeks ago. It indicates that an eve-of-election comeback for Prime Minister John Major after Britain's longest campaign in living memory is almost impossible.

According to the poll results, adjusted by NOP to reflect the likely voting pattern of waverers and people who say they "don't know", Labour will get 50 percent of the vote on Thursday, one point down on the last Reuters/NOP poll.
Labour's march on the Conservatives was also reflected in a widening of their lead on the poll's key question of which party voters most trusted to run the economy.

Labour pulled nine percentage points ahead with 36 percent support on that issue versus 27 percent for Major's Conservatives. In the last Reuters-NOP poll on April 7, Labour's margin over the Conservatives was just five points.

In the poll, conducted on Tuesday, NOP asked likely voters in 52 parliamentary constituencies how they would vote. The adjusted results put the Conservatives' share of support two percentage points down on 28 percent and the Liberal Democrats up by three points to 14 percent since the last Reuters/NOP poll.
The results closely followed the trend of other opinion polls published in the last few days.

"If we get the result which is indicated by the opinion polls, we will have had one of the most significant election results in British political history," said John Benyon, professor of politics at the University of Leicester.

Under Britain's first-past-the-post voting system, the poll results suggest that Tony Blair's Labour party would win 441 seats in the new 659-seat lower House of Commons, making an absolute majority over all other parties of 223.
The Conservative representation in parliament would plunge to just 151 seats and the Liberal Democrats would take 41 places, the figures suggest.
Discounting periods of national government during World War Two, no party has come close to such a commanding majority since Stanley Baldwin led the Conservatives to a 223-seat majority in 1924.

There were few crumbs of comfort for the Conservative party in the poll -- even a hope expressed recently by senior Conservative officials that last-minute waverers would opt for the ruling party seemed unfounded.

"There is little sign that the Labour vote is any shakier than the Conservatives," said Nick Moon, head of political research at NOP. "Most of the changes in the figures since the last poll are insignificant, and could be down to sampling error."

The size of the projected election outcome was at odds with a Reuters survey of some of Britain's top political experts, also published on Wednesday, which gave an average prediction for Labour's majority of just 92 seats.

A majority of the experts said they had toned down their forecasts as they feared the public opinion polls had overestimated the size of Labour's expected majority, making the same mistake as they did five years ago.
During the 1992 election, most pollsters predicted a narrow Labour win and came under heavy criticism when the real outcome gave the Conservatives a fourth term in office.

"Most people find it difficult to believe that Labour could get that sort of vote across the country...The figures are unimaginable -- which is why you get a healthy degree of scepticism among the experts," Benyon told Reuters.

But the level of wavering among those who had made their decision seemed relatively low -- 67 percent of those who expressed a party preference said they were certain to vote for that party, and of the 16 percent who said they were still open to a change of mind, a relatively large number were lukewarm supporters of the third-placed Liberal Democrats.
NOP questioned a representative sample of 1,093 voters.
The state of Britain's health service and its future prospects will be the crucial issue weighing on people's minds as they enter the polling booths, the poll showed.
The second most important issue identified by voters was education, which Labour has billed as its number one priority.

The row over Europe which raged last week and which provoked some of the stormiest moments of the marathon campaign has receded in voters' minds, the poll showed, with just 19 percent saying it was the most important factor to influence their decision.
And 53 percent of those polled said the European debate would not affect the way they mean to vote at all.
